🚨🇲🇽 <u>17 Mexicans dead in Trump's ICE machine — Mexico is filing charges</u>

Mexico's Foreign Ministry has filed 20 formal complaints — 12 before US district prosecutors, 8 before state prosecutors — over the deaths of 17 Mexican nationals under ICE custody or during raids since Trump took office, 14 of them while detained. Foreign Secretary Roberto Velasco says the UN High Commissioner referred all 17 cases to the Human Rights Council for independent review — a response that stands in sharp contrast to the silence from US authorities.

🥚🇲🇽 <u>The real price of the huevo</u>

Egg prices in Mexico jumped 7.92% in the first half of August — the sharpest rise in 20 years, per INEGI — making eggs the single biggest contributor to national inflation this period. The driver: the cost of imported US yellow corn and soymeal used to feed the hens, plus border effects and fuel. Mexicans eat 345 eggs a year on average, and the lowest-income families spend more than half their income on food.

🇲🇽💧 <u>Free the water defenders</u>

More than 80 organizations and Nobel Peace laureate Adolfo Pérez Esquivel are demanding freedom for Rodrigo and Modesto León Jacinto, campesinos of the CECOP jailed in Acapulco since December 2022. Their movement spent over 20 years defending the Papagayo River and defeated the La Parota dam — the megaproject that would have displaced thousands. Their defense says the charges "lack any real legal basis." Guerrero has held them for nearly three years.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>Six years for an apology</u>

On March 21, 2020, municipal police in Tlaxiaco, Oaxaca shot Ángel Daniel Bautista Vázquez in the leg and tortured him until he lost consciousness — asphyxiation, beatings, two fractured legs. Six years later the state finally offered a public apology, after the UN Committee Against Torture ruled Mexico had violated Articles 12 and 13 of the Convention Against Torture. Bautista's answer: the apology "must not remain empty discourse." Only one officer has been charged, and the trial is still pending.

🇲🇽🚲 <u>Ecobici reaches the barrios</u>

Mexico City's public bike system Ecobici will grow 60% — from 9,308 to about 15,000 bikes plus 1,111 new stations — reaching the working-class boroughs of Iztapalapa, Iztacalco and Tlalpan for the first time, Mayor Clara Brugada announced. The system already moves more than 24 million trips a year for some 180,000 users, and under the new 10-year contract every bike and station becomes public property. Broken bikes, Brugada added, "will not be paid" to the operator.

🇲🇽🏭 <u>Tariffs didn't break the economy</u>

While Washington keeps 25% tariffs on Mexican autos and 50% on steel, President Sheinbaum says the economy is going "muy bien" and the second half of 2026 will be even better — driven by Plan México, which is consolidating public and mixed investment in infrastructure to strengthen the domestic market rather than leaning on exports to the US.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>No ballot for fugitives</u>

The man eyeing a run for president is a fugitive. Mexico's presidency confirmed that ex-Tamaulipas governor Francisco García Cabeza de Vaca — wanted by the Attorney General's Office for organized crime and illicit operations, with his extradition requested from the US — cannot be a candidate: Article 38 of the Constitution strips the political rights of anyone who flees an arrest warrant. "A fugitive from justice cannot be a candidate," said presidential legal chief Arturo Zaldívar.
📋 MAÑANERA BREAKDOWN — Complete topic-by-topic recap of Claudia Sheinbaum’s Aug 28 press conference.

🚨🇲🇽 Enforcing immigration law is one thing. Racism against Mexicans is another — and the US must not confuse them. "The vindication of our paisanas and paisanos is deeply relevant right now." — Claudia Sheinbaum, mañanera, Aug 28 2026 About 37.3 million people of Mexican origin live in the US. Sheinbaum drew a hard line: the application of migration laws “must not be confused with racism or discrimination toward Mexicans living abroad,” and demanded respect and recognition for the migrant community.

🇲🇽🎨 Mexico is building a cultural bridge to its diaspora — and steering youth music away from glorifying the cartels. "Songs about love, heartbreak, love of country — not violence, not drugs." — Claudia Sheinbaum, mañanera, Aug 28 2026 México Canta has two goals: connect young Mexican-Americans — first, second and third generation — with youth in Mexico, and shift musical narratives away from violence and addiction. Semifinals were held in the US; the final is in Mazatlán.
